Revolut discloses data breach exposing financial info, passports

Revolut disclosed that attackers impersonating a government agency used a spoofed, authenticated email request to obtain highly sensitive customer data, including identity documents, selfies, account statements, and transaction histories. The company says customer funds and systems were not affected and that only a limited, potentially high-net-worth group was targeted.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Revolut disclosed that it shared customer information with a threat actor who impersonated a government agency through an unauthorized email account using the agency’s official domain.
  • 02The company said the email carried valid domain-authentication credentials, leading it to fulfill the request under the belief that it was legitimate.
  • 03The disclosed data includes identity and contact details, passport or driver’s-license copies, facial-verification images, account statements with IBANs, withdrawal records, and full transaction histories including Bitcoin transactions.
  • 04Revolut said the incident affected a very limited number of customers, although it did not disclose the exact number, and stated that its systems and customer funds were unaffected.
  • 05Revolut said it blocked the email address after detecting the incident and notified the relevant government agency, law enforcement, data-protection authorities, and financial regulators.

Revolut disclosed a data breach in which it shared customer information with a threat actor impersonating a government agency. The request arrived from an unauthorized email account using the agency’s official domain and carried valid domain-authentication credentials, so Revolut fulfilled it believing it was legitimate. Revolut operates in more than 160 countries and regions and serves over 80 million customers, but said this incident affected a “very limited” number of people without providing an exact count.

The disclosed data may include names, dates of birth, occupations, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, passport or driver’s-license copies, and facial-verification selfies. It also includes account statements with IBAN numbers, withdrawal records, and full transaction histories, including Bitcoin transactions. Revolut said its systems and customer funds were not affected; after detecting the incident, it blocked the email address and notified the relevant government agency, law-enforcement bodies, data-protection authorities, and financial regulators.

  • The fraudulent request appeared credible because it was sent from an unauthorized mailbox using an official government domain and carried valid domain-authentication credentials.
  • The information disclosed combined identity-document copies and facial-verification selfies with detailed banking and transaction records, including Bitcoin transactions.
  • Although Revolut described the affected population as very limited, crypto fraud investigator ZachXBT said the apparent targeting was focused on high-net-worth users.
  • This is Revolut’s second disclosed customer-data breach in four years, following a September 2022 incident affecting 50,150 customers.

Revolut gave sensitive information about an undisclosed, reportedly small number of customers to criminals who pretended to be a government agency in an email. The stolen information may include names, contact details, passport or driver’s-license copies, account statements, and full payment histories, including Bitcoin activity. Revolut says its systems and customers’ money were not affected, but the exposed documents and financial details could put affected people at risk of fraud or impersonation; an investigator said the victims may have been wealthy users.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete breach at a major global fintech provider involving identity documents, biometric verification images, account statements, and transaction histories. The affected group is reportedly limited, but the sensitivity of the exposed data and the use of a convincing fake government request make it broadly relevant.

Homebrew 7.0.0 gets built-in GUI, better security controls

Homebrew 7.0.0 adds a native macOS BrewUI interface, a brew vulns command backed by Homebrew-specific advisories and OSV data, and stronger sandboxing defaults. The release also improves install and upgrade speed through concurrent package processing.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Homebrew 7.0.0 releases BrewUI, a native graphical interface for macOS 26 Tahoe and later that lets users browse, search, inspect, and manage package dependencies.
  • 02The new brew vulns command can scan installed formulae, a specified formula, or formulae and dependencies listed in a Brewfile for known security issues.
  • 03Homebrew queries OSV.dev using upstream repository and version information, verifies potential matches, applies optional severity filters, and checks whether Homebrew has already patched the affected formula.
  • 04Homebrew has published a Homebrew-specific advisory database in OSV format to record issues affecting formula versions and revisions, including fixes backported without changing the upstream version.
  • 05Version 7.0.0 blocks access to users’ home directories by default, separates network-enabled downloads from offline installation, and speeds installations and upgrades through concurrent package processing.

Homebrew 7.0.0 has been released with BrewUI, a native graphical interface available on macOS 26 Tahoe and later. BrewUI allows users to browse and search packages and to inspect and manage dependencies. Homebrew is a widely used open-source package manager for macOS, and threat actors have previously targeted its users through clone websites and ClickFix lures that deliver information-stealing malware.

The release adds the brew vulns command, which can scan installed formulae, a specific formula, or formulae and dependencies declared in a Brewfile. It queries OSV.dev with upstream repository and version information, verifies potential matches, supports severity filters, and checks whether Homebrew has already applied a security patch. Homebrew also introduced an OSV-format advisory database covering affected formula versions and revisions, including backported fixes that do not change the upstream version.

Homebrew 7.0.0 improves sandboxing by blocking access to users’ home directories by default and separating network-enabled dependency downloads from offline installation. The project also says installations and upgrades are faster because packages can be downloaded, prepared, and installed concurrently. These changes add package security checks and stronger installation controls while improving usability and performance.

  • Homebrew’s advisory database can distinguish an unresolved upstream issue from one that Homebrew has already fixed through a backport, even when the software’s upstream version number has not changed.
  • The brew vulns scanner checks both installed formulae and the dependency lists defined in a Brewfile, allowing users to assess software before or alongside installation planning.
  • Homebrew’s new sandboxing approach separates internet-enabled dependency downloads from offline installation and blocks access to users’ home directories by default.
  • Because threat actors have used fake Homebrew sites and deceptive ClickFix prompts to distribute information-stealing malware, users should be aware that Homebrew’s popularity has made it a recurring target for impersonation.

Homebrew, a popular tool for installing software on Macs, has released version 7.0.0 with a new visual app for finding and managing software. It can now check installed software for known security problems and better limits what installation processes can access on a user’s computer. This matters to Mac users because Homebrew is widely used and has been targeted by criminals who try to trick people into installing harmful software through fake websites and deceptive prompts.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Homebrew 7.0.0 is a concrete security-relevant release for a widely used macOS package manager, adding vulnerability scanning, advisory data, and stronger sandboxing. It is useful for organizations and users that rely on Homebrew, but the article does not report active exploitation or an urgent critical flaw requiring immediate action.

These apps can be given permission to read or use company information, so the risk affects organizations and their employees who use Google Workspace. Microsoft: September updates break audio on some Windows PCs

Microsoft confirmed that September 2026 Windows 11 security updates KB5124008 and KB5124012 can cause USB Audio Class 1.0 devices to fail or produce no sound on version 24H2 and later. No official workaround is available yet, though switching affected devices to 2-channel audio has helped some users.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft confirmed that the September 2026 security updates KB5124008 and KB5124012 can cause some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices to fail to start or produce no sound.
  • 02The issue affects only Windows 11 version 24H2 or later systems using USB Audio Class 1.0 devices.
  • 03Affected users have reported Device Manager Code 10 errors, no audio output, and unresponsive volume controls and sound settings.
  • 04Some affected USB speakers fail only when multichannel features such as 3D audio or 8-channel modes are used.
  • 05Microsoft has not provided an official workaround, but some users restored audio by switching to 2-channel mode.

Microsoft confirmed that the September 2026 Windows security updates KB5124008 and KB5124012 can cause some USB audio devices to fail or produce no sound. The known issue is limited to USB Audio Class 1.0 devices on systems running Windows 11 version 24H2 or later. Affected users have reported Device Manager messages stating that the device cannot start with Code 10, along with no audio output and unresponsive volume controls or sound settings.

Some impacted USB speakers reportedly fail only when multichannel capabilities, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes, are enabled. Microsoft has not provided an official workaround, but some users have restored audio by switching devices to 2-channel mode. The issue follows several earlier Windows 11 24H2 audio-related problems involving USB audio drivers, Dirac audio improvement software, incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology drivers, and USB DAC systems.

  • The reported problem is limited to USB Audio Class 1.0 devices, rather than affecting all audio hardware on Windows 11.
  • Multichannel settings appear to be an important trigger for some users, as certain USB speakers fail only with 3D audio or 8-channel modes enabled.
  • Switching an affected device to 2-channel audio has restored sound for some users despite Microsoft not yet publishing an official workaround.
  • The issue follows earlier Windows 11 24H2 audio problems involving USB audio drivers, Dirac audio software, Intel Smart Sound Technology drivers, and USB DAC systems.

Microsoft says its September 2026 Windows updates can stop some USB-connected speakers and other sound devices from working properly. The problem affects people using Windows 11 version 24H2 or newer with older USB audio devices, causing no sound, broken volume controls, or a message saying the device cannot start. Microsoft has not provided a fix yet, although switching the device to basic two-speaker sound has helped some people. This matters because updates meant to improve security can also unexpectedly disrupt everyday functions such as audio on affected computers.

CISA: Hackers now exploit max severity GitLab flaw in attacks

CISA has added CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity GitLab path traversal flaw that enables unauthenticated arbitrary file reads, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after attacks began. Organizations should immediately upgrade GitLab CE/EE to versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6, or 19.1 and review logs for suspicious repository commits API requests.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CISA added CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity GitLab flaw, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after it was observed being used in attacks.
  • 02The flaw affects GitLab's repository commits API and can allow unauthenticated attackers to read credentials, secrets, and other sensitive files from vulnerable servers.
  • 03GitLab fixed the issue in Community Edition and Enterprise Edition versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6, and 19.1, and urged users to patch immediately.
  • 04CISA gave federal agencies three days to secure affected systems under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 and encouraged all organizations to prioritize remediation.
  • 05watchTowr advised defenders to review logs for HTTP POST requests to repository commits API addresses containing file.path parameters as potential signs of attempted exploitation.

CISA warned that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability, and added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The flaw affects GitLab’s repository commits API because authentication is not properly enforced and file paths are not sufficiently restricted. An unauthenticated attacker can use it to read credentials, secrets, and other sensitive information from vulnerable GitLab servers. GitLab’s platform is used by more than half of Fortune 100 companies and has over 30 million registered users worldwide.

GitLab released fixes for Community Edition and Enterprise Edition in versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6, and 19.1, urging customers to patch immediately. watchTowr reported observing Internet-wide probes for the flaw one day after the fixes were released and said arbitrary files could be read with a single HTTP request. It advised defenders to examine logs for HTTP POST requests to repository commits API URLs containing file.path parameters. Federal agencies were given three days to address the issue under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, while CISA urged all organizations to prioritize remediation.

  • Internet-wide probing for the flaw was observed only one day after GitLab released fixes, indicating that unpatched systems were being targeted almost immediately.
  • The issue can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files with a single HTTP request, potentially exposing credentials and other secrets without needing an account.
  • Organizations can look for possible exploitation attempts by checking logs for HTTP POST requests to repository commits API URLs containing file.path parameters.
  • Although GitLab had not yet labeled the flaw as actively exploited, CISA added it to its actively exploited catalog and imposed a three-day remediation deadline for federal agencies.

U.S. officials say attackers are already using a serious flaw in GitLab, a widely used platform where organizations store and manage software code. The flaw can let someone who is not signed in read sensitive files, including passwords and secret access information, from unpatched GitLab systems. GitLab has released fixes, and the issue matters because GitLab is used by more than half of Fortune 100 companies and over 30 million registered users worldwide.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

CISA reports active exploitation of a maximum-severity GitLab flaw that can let unauthenticated attackers read arbitrary files, including credentials and secrets. GitLab is widely deployed, patches are available, and CISA gave federal agencies only three days to remediate.

Optional · 35 sponsored 14 Sep 2026 14:01 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Why Patch Automation Needs Brakes, Not Just an Accelerator

Action1 argues that patch automation should use staged deployment rings, predefined health criteria, and stop conditions to prevent faulty updates from rapidly spreading across an organization. Human approval should remain for critical systems while routine, proven deployments progress automatically.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The growing volume and frequency of software updates can force IT teams to shorten or skip testing as patch backlogs grow.
  • 02The article argues that automation should include controls that determine where and when an update is deployed, what is checked before it progresses, and when deployment stops.
  • 03Staged deployment sends updates first to small, representative groups and expands them only after predefined conditions such as successful installation, healthy endpoints, functioning applications, and acceptable failure rates are met.
  • 04The article recommends keeping human review for business-critical systems such as domain controllers, production databases, and ERP workloads while automating routine decisions that have clear criteria.
  • 05Action1 promotes its Update Rings feature, manual approval workflows, and endpoint groups as tools for controlled patch deployment.

Patch-management workloads are increasing as vendors release fixes for browsers, operating systems, applications, and infrastructure, while IT teams face limited staff, competing priorities, and complex environments. The article warns that growing backlogs can lead organizations to shorten testing or move updates directly into production. It argues that automation should not be measured only by deployment speed, because a faulty update can be distributed to thousands of endpoints as quickly as a successful one.

The article recommends staged deployment through increasingly larger endpoint groups, beginning with IT staff or representative systems. Updates should move forward only when predefined checks show that installation succeeded, endpoints remain healthy, applications continue working, and failure rates are acceptable; otherwise, deployment should stop. It says human judgment should remain for business-critical workloads such as domain controllers, production databases, and ERP systems, while routine decisions with clear criteria can be automated. Action1 promotes its Update Rings, endpoint groups, and manual approval workflows as tools for implementing this controlled deployment model.

  • Automation can amplify harm as quickly as it improves efficiency: a bad update can reach 10,000 endpoints just as rapidly as a good one.
  • A traditional test lab cannot reproduce every combination of production hardware, software, configuration, and user behavior, so controlled deployment to selected production systems can serve as part of validation.
  • The article frames automation maturity as automating defined decisions rather than eliminating people: administrators should set policy and escalation criteria while retaining judgment where consequences are significant.
  • Concentrated larger environments may allow organizations to designate less mission-critical systems as canaries for early deployments before broader rollout.

The article says organizations face a growing stream of software updates and security fixes, while their technology teams have limited time to test and install them. It recommends sending updates first to a small group of computers, checking that they work properly, and only then expanding to more systems while automatically stopping if problems appear. This matters because a bad update can disrupt thousands of computers just as quickly as a good update can protect them, especially for important systems such as company databases and business software.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is sponsored, evergreen best-practice commentary on controlled patch automation rather than reporting a specific incident, vulnerability, or urgent update. It may offer useful operational ideas, but it has low urgency and limited novelty for security professionals.

Japan's Digital Agency says VPN flaw exposed 246,000 personnel records

Japan’s Digital Agency says attackers exploited a known, medium-severity VPN flaw to access a government system, potentially exposing roughly 246,000 personnel-data records. The agency contained the intrusion and says it has found no confirmed misuse or impact on public services.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Japan’s Digital Agency said an attacker exploited a known, medium-severity flaw in a VPN device used by the Government Solution Service to gain unauthorized system access.
  • 02The agency began investigating on June 25 after detecting large-scale file access from a maintenance and operations staff member’s account, and it contained the incident on July 9 by suspending the account and isolating the compromised equipment.
  • 03Potentially exposed data included approximately 236,000 names, 231,000 email addresses, 94,000 telephone numbers, and 1,000 physical addresses.
  • 04Affected people include government employees, public officials, and businesses and individuals using the Government Solution Service, while the agency said general-public data, My Number identifiers, bank details, and pension numbers were not exposed.
  • 05The agency reported no detected misuse of the information, no disruption to government services, and no confirmed impact on other systems.

Japan’s Digital Agency said an attacker exploited a vulnerability in a VPN device used by the Government Solution Service (GSS) to gain unauthorized access to a system. The agency began investigating on June 25 after detecting large-scale file access through a maintenance and operations staff member’s account. On July 9, it suspended that account and cut off external communications from the compromised equipment. The agency said the flaw was medium severity and not a zero-day, but did not identify the VPN product or vulnerability involved.

The incident may have exposed around 246,000 rows of personnel-related information, including approximately 236,000 names, 231,000 email addresses, 94,000 phone numbers, and 1,000 physical addresses. Those potentially affected include government employees, public officials, and associated businesses and individuals that use GSS; the agency said general-public data, My Number identifiers, bank details, and pension numbers were not exposed. It reported no detected misuse of the information, no confirmed impact on other systems, and no interruption to government services. However, it warned affected people about increased impersonation and phishing risks and said it would contact them directly.

  • The intrusion was discovered through unusually large-scale file access from a maintenance worker’s account, showing that the attacker’s activity appeared under a legitimate account rather than being identified solely at the point of entry.
  • Although the exposed records did not include My Number identifiers, bank-account details, or pension numbers, the agency specifically warned that the contact information could increase impersonation and phishing risks.
  • The affected flaw was rated medium severity and was not a zero-day, yet it was sufficient to enable unauthorized access to a government system.
  • The agency said public disclosure was delayed because determining how the intruder entered, which information may have been affected, and who was affected was complex.

Japan’s Digital Agency says someone used a known weakness in a remote-access system to enter a government network and may have viewed about 246,000 records about employees and related people. The information could include names, email addresses, phone numbers, and some home addresses, affecting government workers, public officials, and businesses or individuals connected to the system. While no misuse has been found and the public’s identification, bank, and pension details were not involved, the exposed contact information could be used for convincing scams or impersonation attempts.

This is a significant government-system breach affecting approximately 246,000 personnel-data records and involving exploitation of a known VPN-device flaw. It is broadly relevant as an example of real-world exploitation and phishing risk, though the affected product and vulnerability were not identified.

Twitch extension with 30K installs exposes users’ OAuth tokens

The Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot browser extension, installed by more than 30,000 users, reportedly sends Twitch OAuth session tokens to JeetBot-controlled proxy servers by placing them in logged URL parameters. Users should remove the extension and revoke all active Twitch sessions to invalidate potentially exposed tokens.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot extension, available through the official Chrome and Firefox stores, has more than 30,000 installs and advertises ad blocking, 1080p playback, region restriction bypassing, and channel-point collection.
  • 02Socket reported that the extension captures the Twitch web client’s authorization header, extracts the user’s OAuth token, and sends it through proxy servers operated by JeetBot.
  • 03The current extension versions append the token as an auth URL parameter on redirected Twitch video playlist requests, causing the token to be recorded in proxy-server request logs.
  • 04The extension performs this token-forwarding process for every Twitch channel watched except ten Russian-language channels hardcoded into its code.
  • 05Socket recommends that affected users remove the extension, disconnect all Twitch sessions, and re-authenticate to invalidate tokens that may have been forwarded.

A browser extension called Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot, available in the official Chrome and Firefox stores, has more than 30,000 installs and claims to block ads, enable 1080p playback, bypass region restrictions, and collect channel points. Socket reported that the extension captures the authorization header used by Twitch’s web client, extracts the user’s OAuth session token, and sends it through proxy servers operated by JeetBot. JeetBot is described as a commercial Russian-language streaming and chatbot service for Twitch, Kick, and VK Live.

According to Socket, current versions append the token as an auth= parameter when redirecting Twitch video playlist requests through a proxy. Because the token is included in the web address, it is written in clear text to the proxy server’s request logs, where the software vendor can retrieve it. The behavior reportedly occurs for every channel a user watches except ten Russian-language channels hardcoded into the extension. Socket recommends removing the extension, disconnecting all Twitch sessions, and signing in again to invalidate any tokens that may have been forwarded.

  • The extension’s Chrome Web Store privacy disclosure says the developer will not collect or use user data, despite Socket’s finding that Twitch OAuth tokens are sent through JeetBot-operated proxy servers.
  • Putting OAuth tokens in URL parameters makes them available in ordinary proxy request logs, meaning the service operator can retrieve them without needing a separate token-collection system.
  • The extension excludes ten hardcoded Russian-language channels from the token-forwarding behavior, indicating that the behavior is not applied uniformly to every viewed channel.
  • The developer’s Firefox Add-ons description acknowledges that earlier versions transmitted users’ Twitch OAuth tokens to its server and described this as necessary for higher-resolution streaming.
  • Despite the reported risks, the extension remained available in both the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-Ons store at the time of publication.

A Twitch browser add-on called Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot, used by more than 30,000 people, was found to send users’ Twitch login session keys to servers run by its developer. Those keys can let someone act as the user on Twitch, and the add-on reportedly put them into web addresses where the server operator could easily find them in its records. Users should remove the add-on, sign out of all Twitch sessions, and sign in again so any previously shared keys stop working.

It is actionable for affected users and relevant to browser-extension and credential-handling risks, though the article does not report active exploitation of the exposed tokens.

Microsoft released emergency out-of-band updates on September 14 to fix Remote Desktop Services (RDS) failures caused by the September 2026 Windows security updates. Affected systems experienced Remote Desktop Protocol connection and sign-in failures, and some servers became unresponsive. Related tools, including Microsoft Management Console, RDS Licensing Diagnoser, File Explorer, and the Windows Update page, could also stop responding. Administrators had previously reported that uninstalling the September updates restored Remote Desktop functionality, but removed the security fixes included with them.

The updates cover Windows 10 21H2 and 22H2, Windows 11 24H2, 25H2, and 26H1, and Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. The Windows Server fixes address RDS failures introduced by KB5122871 on Windows Server 2025 and KB5122882 on Windows Server 2022. Microsoft had supplied Group Policy mitigations while developing the permanent fixes, and the Server out-of-band updates are available through the Microsoft Update Catalog.

The Windows 11 out-of-band updates also resolve a Hyper-V issue in which shared Windows host folders could be missing or inaccessible in Linux virtual machines. They additionally address multichannel audio failures involving some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices, including 8-channel and 3D audio modes. However, Microsoft said it is still working on a fix for other USB Audio Class 1.0 problems that can cause devices to fail to start, produce no audio, or show a Code 10 error in Device Manager.

The problem affects several versions of Windows and Windows Server, and could also cause related management tools to freeze. This matters because removing the original security updates could restore remote access but would also remove their security protections.

AI Changed the Exposure Problem. Validation Needs to Change With It.

AI is rapidly increasing vulnerability discovery, making CVSS scores alone insufficient for prioritization; organizations need evidence-based validation of exploitability, control effectiveness, and attack paths in their own environments.   • 03Automated pentesting can prove exploitability and map attack paths, but it cannot always test newly disclosed flaws without working exploits or systems that are unsafe to test live.
  • 04The article argues that exploitability validation, security-control validation, and agentic pentesting should be combined so organizations can prioritize, remediate, and revalidate exposures using connected evidence.
  • 05Picus Security’s Validation Summit ’26, scheduled for October 14–15, will feature presentations and discussions on validation practices from Mikko Hyppönen, Picus, Chanel, Atlassian, and the NFL.

AI is accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, increasing the number of findings that security teams must assess. The article cites 35,853 CVEs published in the first half of 2026, while 495 were catalogued as exploited in the wild and 116 were reportedly attacked on the day of disclosure. It argues that severity scores such as CVSS cannot by themselves show whether a vulnerability is reachable, exploitable, or important to a specific organization.

The article says organizations need connected evidence about exploitability, the effectiveness of their protective and detection controls, and the paths an attacker could take through their environment. Automated or agentic penetration testing can provide strong evidence through real exploits, but it cannot safely cover every system or assess newly disclosed CVEs that lack a working exploit. Picus advocates combining exploitability validation, security-control validation, and agentic pentesting, and will present this approach at its Validation Summit ’26 on October 14 and 15.

  • Despite 95% of organizations ranking pentesting as a top or high priority, Omdia research cited in the article found that organizations test only 32% of their average attack surface each year.
  • A vulnerability’s priority can change as new evidence emerges, so the article recommends connecting validation results to remediation decisions and rechecking exposures after fixes rather than treating ticket closure as final proof of resolution.

The article says AI is helping uncover software flaws much faster, creating far more warnings than organizations can realistically treat as urgent. Most flaws are never used by criminals, and the same flaw can be harmless on one company’s system but serious on another’s depending on whether it can be reached and what protections are in place. It argues that companies should test which warnings could actually be used against their own important systems, whether their defenses would stop them, and whether a problem could help an intruder move farther through the organization. This matters because better testing can help businesses focus limited time on the small number of problems most likely to cause real damage.

Security researchers at ExPatch found that Telegram Desktop could place unescaped text from bot message buttons into HTML chat exports, allowing hidden JavaScript to run when an exported file was opened in a browser. The malicious message could appear ordinary or empty in Telegram, using invisible characters to conceal the code. The script could copy messages and chat details from the opened export to an attacker-controlled server or alter the page’s displayed contents.

The issue affected Telegram Desktop versions 4.15.1 through 6.9.3 and was fixed in 6.9.4 beta and 7.0.1 stable. A bot message with web-link buttons could retain the malicious content when forwarded into another group, where it could remain in history until a later export. A flaw in Telegram Desktop allowed a bot to hide harmful code inside an ordinary-looking message button, which could run later if a chat was saved as an HTML file and opened in a web browser. The code could copy messages from that saved file to an attacker or change what the file displays, such as showing a fake Telegram verification form. Telegram fixed the app in July, but people with chat exports made using older versions may still be affected unless they create new exports or open the old files with JavaScript turned off.

New DDRop Attack Breaks Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP Confidential Computing

Researchers demonstrated DDRop, a low-cost physical interposer attack that silently drops DDR5 memory writes and exploits missing freshness protections to undermine Intel TDX, Scalable SGX, and AMD SEV-SNP confidential computing. The attack requires prior software control and brief physical access to install hardware, and fully fixing the underlying flaw would require redesigned memory-encryption hardware.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Researchers disclosed DDRop, an active DDR5 memory interposer attack that silently drops writes so processors can read older encrypted memory contents as if they were current.
  • 02DDRop affects Intel TDX, Intel Scalable SGX, and AMD SEV-SNP, and requires an attacker to control server software and briefly gain physical access to install an interposer between the processor and a memory module.
  • 03On Intel TDX, the researchers used dropped page-table writes to read and modify protected virtual-machine memory, enable debug mode, and alter launch measurements used for remote attestation.
  • 04On AMD SEV-SNP, the researchers used dropped writes during page relocation to copy the contents of one victim memory page into another.
  • 05The researchers said there is no simple patch because the underlying weakness is the lack of a memory freshness check, and a complete fix would require new memory-encryption hardware with integrity and freshness protections.

Researchers disclosed DDRop, a hardware attack that silently drops DDR5 memory writes, causing a processor to read older encrypted data as though it were current. It affects Intel TDX, Intel Scalable SGX, and AMD SEV-SNP confidential-computing technologies, which encrypt server memory but omit checks that confirm data is the newest version. The attack requires an adversary who already controls server software and can briefly access the system physically to install a small interposer board between the processor and a memory module. The researchers estimate the hardware parts cost about $159 and say it can be installed in minutes.

The interposer forces an error on the memory command bus and then prevents the memory module from reporting that error, causing the memory module to discard a write without the processor knowing. On Intel TDX, researchers used this capability to manipulate page-table setup, access protected virtual-machine memory, enable debug mode, and alter launch measurements used for remote attestation. On AMD SEV-SNP, they demonstrated copying one victim memory page into another during page relocation. The researchers said there is no simple patch because fully addressing the missing freshness protection would require new memory-encryption hardware, although software changes may raise the difficulty of exploitation.

  • DDRop bypasses DDR5’s defenses against earlier address-swapping interposer attacks by causing a memory command error and then preventing the memory module from reporting that error to the processor.
  • Intel TDX’s optional cryptographic-integrity mode would block some demonstrated cross-virtual-machine attacks, but the researchers argue it would not prevent an attacker from forging its own machine’s attestation because stale data can still be reused.
  • The attack hardware is estimated to cost about $159 in parts, can be installed in minutes, and can then be operated entirely through software.
  • Intel Client SGX is not affected because it uses a hardware integrity tree that detects stale memory contents, while NVIDIA confidential-computing GPUs are out of reach because their memory is inside the chip package.

Researchers found that someone who already controls a server’s software and can briefly tamper with its hardware could use a cheap device to make the server ignore some memory updates. This can let old data appear current, undermining protections used by Intel and AMD systems to keep cloud customers’ data private even from the cloud provider. The main risk is to cloud servers using Intel TDX, Intel Scalable SGX, or AMD SEV-SNP, not ordinary home computers or phones. Fixing the root problem likely requires future hardware designs, although software changes may make the attack harder.

This is a significant, concrete research finding affecting Intel and AMD confidential-computing technologies used by major cloud platforms. Although it requires prior software control and brief physical access and has no reported in-the-wild use, it exposes a hardware-level weakness with no simple complete fix.

A cross-store browser extension named Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot leaked Twitch OAuth tokens associated with nearly 31,000 Chrome and Firefox users to proxy servers operated by a Russian commercial bot service. The Chrome extension had about 30,000 users and the Firefox add-on had 604 users when the article was written. Socket researcher Kush Pandya said the tokens were forwarded for every channel watched except a hardcoded allowlist of ten Twitch channels, most of them Russian-language streamers.

The extension redirected Twitch video-playlist requests through operator-controlled proxies and included the user’s token as an &auth= URL parameter. Because the token was in the URL, it was written in cleartext to the proxy servers’ request logs; the token could provide access to chat, private messages, account settings, and channel points. JeetBot’s documentation says Firefox version 85.8.7 no longer sends tokens to its proxies and advises users to update or disable older versions, but it warns that doing so does not revoke tokens already transmitted.

  • Because the extension placed Twitch access tokens directly in URL parameters, the tokens were recorded in cleartext in the proxy servers’ request logs.
  • The extension exempted a hardcoded list of ten mostly Russian-language streamer channels from token forwarding, while sending tokens for viewers of other channels.
  • Earlier version 4.x builds reportedly sent tokens to a dedicated operator endpoint and used backup endpoints on deno.dev and deno.net.
  • Updating or disabling the extension stops further token transmission but does not invalidate tokens that were already sent to the operator’s infrastructure.

A browser add-on called Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot sent the account access keys of nearly 31,000 Twitch users to servers controlled by its operator while they watched streams. Those keys could let whoever has them use a person’s Twitch account without knowing the password, including reading or sending private messages, chatting, changing settings, and spending channel points. The add-on’s developer says newer Firefox versions no longer send the keys, but people using older versions remain exposed until they update or disable it, and keys sent in the past are not automatically cancelled.

WordPress Adds Automated Plugin Reviews to Block High-Risk Updates Before Distribution

WordPress now automatically scans every plugin and theme update during a six-hour cooldown period, blocking releases with high-risk security scores before they reach users through the WordPress.org update API.
KEY POINTS
  • 01WordPress is launching automated security reviews for every plugin release before distribution through the WordPress.org update API.
  • 02During a six-hour cooldown period, WordPress analyzes plugin and theme release changes using AI models and Jetpack Scan, then combines results into a security score.
  • 03Releases with high-risk scores are automatically blocked, and plugin committers receive an email describing the findings.
  • 04WordPress said its automated review detected a backdoor in a July 28, 2026 plugin release affecting a plugin with about 20,000 active installations, and the compromised version was not distributed through the update API.
  • 05Developers can address a blocked release by fixing the identified issues and publishing a new version that scores below the high-risk threshold.

WordPress is launching an automated security review for every plugin release before it is distributed through the WordPress.org update API. The system is intended to address the gap between a developer committing an update and the update reaching downstream users, where a previously safe plugin could introduce a security flaw or harmful code. Plugin and theme releases already undergo a cooldown period before automatic distribution under the Protect The Shire initiative, which is currently set to six hours.

During that cooldown period, WordPress analyzes release changes using AI models and Jetpack Scan, cross-checks the results, and assigns a security risk score. Releases above the high-risk threshold are automatically blocked without Plugins Team involvement, while lower-risk releases continue through the normal process; committers are emailed only when their release is blocked. WordPress said this process detected a backdoor in a July 28, 2026 release for a plugin with about 20,000 active installations, preventing the compromised version from being distributed through the update API.

  • WordPress’s prior review process covered new plugins entering the directory, but not the continuous updates released afterward, creating an opportunity for a previously safe plugin to later distribute harmful code.
  • A high-risk score can result from accidental security mistakes as well as deliberately harmful code, so an automatic block is not necessarily an accusation of malicious intent.
  • The six-hour delay before automatic distribution was reduced from the initiative’s original 24-hour period, balancing time for checks against the speed at which developers can deliver updates.
  • For blocked releases, publishing a corrected version is usually faster for developers than requesting a manual review from the Plugins Team.
  • The automated review can block a risky release without Plugins Team involvement, allowing potentially dangerous updates to be stopped before they are distributed.

WordPress is adding an automatic safety check for every new version of a plugin or theme before it is sent to users through its update system. The check can stop updates that appear to contain harmful code or serious mistakes, protecting website owners and visitors from unsafe software. This matters because a compromised update for a plugin used by thousands of sites was recently prevented from being distributed, showing how trusted updates can otherwise become a way to spread harm.

A phishing email was sent to an equipment rental company’s internal accounting group, which automatically forwarded it to four employees and made it appear to have passed through the company’s own email system. Unmasking Cloud Identities: From Behavioral Clustering to Automated Detection

Unit 42 shows that cloud identities can be reliably mapped to functional roles by clustering their AWS CloudTrail API behavior rather than trusting names or assigned permissions. The resulting behavioral baselines can be distilled into lightweight SQL-compatible detection logic to flag anomalous activity, such as a backup identity performing administrative actions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Unit 42 analyzed two months of AWS CloudTrail activity from more than 40,000 identities across 125 cloud environments to map identities to functional roles based on observed behavior.
  • 02The research distinguishes an identity’s assigned permissions from its actual API activity, noting that names and IAM policies may not reveal an identity’s true role and can be used to mask malicious activity.
  • 03The clustering pipeline represents each identity by the AWS operations it invoked, uses UMAP to reduce the resulting high-dimensional data, and uses HDBSCAN to group identities with similar behavioral patterns.
  • 04The researchers identified reproducible behavioral groups associated with roles including administrators, DevOps, infrastructure-as-code runners, CI/CD systems, security products, backup agents, networking components, and FinOps platforms.
  • 05A sparse logistic-regression classifier with L1 regularization can distill selected behavioral clusters into interpretable, SQL-compatible logic for classifying identities at scale without continuously running the full machine-learning pipeline.

Unit 42 developed a behavioral clustering model to identify the functional roles of cloud identities from AWS CloudTrail audit-log activity rather than from identity names or assigned permissions. The researchers examined more than 40,000 identities across 125 cloud environments over two months and identified recurring groups associated with administrators, DevOps, infrastructure-as-code runners, CI/CD systems, security products, backup agents, networking components and FinOps platforms. This matters because attackers can use benign labels or pre-existing permission profiles to make malicious activity harder to distinguish from legitimate cloud operations.

The model represents each identity according to the AWS API operations it invoked, reduces the resulting high-dimensional data with UMAP, and groups similar identities using HDBSCAN. In a cluster of roughly 5,000 administrative console users, approximately 94% invoked ConsoleLogin, compared with fewer than 1% of identities in any other cluster. Unit 42 then showed that selected clusters can be converted into interpretable logistic-regression logic with L1 regularization and implemented in standard SQL, allowing organizations to classify identities at scale and detect deviations such as a backup identity beginning to perform administrative actions.

  • In the administrative-user cluster of roughly 5,000 identities, about 94% performed AWS ConsoleLogin, while fewer than 1% of identities in any other cluster performed that operation, making it a strong behavioral marker.
  • Operations automatically triggered by the AWS Management Console, such as ListNotificationHubs, can be more distinctive for identifying console users than high-frequency operations alone, as shown by class-based scoring.
  • Recurring identity-name patterns can help validate a behavioral cluster without being trusted as the sole source of truth; the administrator cluster commonly included the AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_ prefix generated by AWS IAM Identity Center.
  • The article demonstrates that a complex clustering model can be translated into a small set of weighted API-operation checks and run directly in standard SQL, avoiding the need to continuously operate a resource-intensive machine-learning pipeline.
  • Behavioral role baselines can expose high-risk deviations that permission reviews may miss, such as a backup-service identity beginning to execute administrative actions.

The article explains a way to study the actions of cloud accounts and determine what jobs they really perform, such as managing systems, running backups, checking security, or supporting software development. The researchers examined more than 40,000 accounts across 125 cloud environments and found that accounts with similar jobs tend to behave in similar ways. This matters to organizations using Amazon Web Services because an attacker may hide behind a normal-looking account name or overly broad access rights, but unusual actions—such as a backup account suddenly acting like an administrator—can reveal the problem. Using these behavior patterns can help security teams find suspicious activity faster and reduce false alarms.

The proposed UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill directly regulates Operators of Essential Services, managed service providers, and data centre operators, but its effects may extend further through supply-chain provisions. It introduces a Designated Critical Supplier category that allows regulators to designate suppliers whose products or services are essential to maintaining an essential service. Designated suppliers would face obligations equivalent to those for Operators of Essential Services, including security standards, incident reporting, regulatory inspection, and turnover-based penalties.

The Bill may also drive regulated organisations to impose security requirements on suppliers through contracts, procurement processes, due-diligence requests, and audit rights. Manufacturers and technology providers supplying energy, water, or other regulated sectors may therefore need to demonstrate their products’ security posture, including known vulnerabilities, network behaviour, update mechanisms, and required access. The article says commercial pressure from customers is likely to affect more organisations and arrive sooner than formal critical-supplier designation, while manufacturers must also assess cyber risks introduced by their own connected suppliers and technology vendors.

  • Commercial pressure is likely to reach far more suppliers, and sooner, than formal designation because regulated customers can immediately add security conditions to procurement and contract processes.
  • The same supply-chain risk issue applies in both directions: manufacturers may be scrutinized by critical-infrastructure customers while also needing to examine what their own suppliers and vendors can access in plant environments.
  • For products used in operational environments, a supplier must be prepared to explain practical details such as how the product behaves on a network, how it is updated, and what access it needs to operate.
  • The article frames early preparation as a business-readiness issue rather than only a compliance exercise, since suppliers may need answers before a customer asks for them.

The proposed UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would not only affect energy, water, transport, and similar essential-service operators; it could also affect the companies that supply them. Suppliers whose products or services are especially important could be formally required to meet security rules, while many more may face tougher customer questionnaires, contract terms, and checks. This matters because manufacturers and technology providers may need to show that their products are safe to use in important facilities and that they understand risks in their own operations and suppliers.

The issue can allow remote code execution on the underlying host when an attacker bypasses the plugin’s object-data safety check using a forged wp_hash value. Public proof-of-concept code is available, although the article states that observed exploitation was low at the time of writing.

The attack requires comments to be enabled and visible on event pages, but it does not require an account, credentials, or administrator action. An unauthenticated visitor can submit malicious block markup as an event-page comment, and WordPress renders the commenter’s pending comment through a moderation-hash URL before a moderator reviews it. All The Events Calendar versions through 6.17.4 are affected, and StellarWP released version 6.17.4.1 on September 10, 2026; organizations should verify exact installed versions, inventory public WordPress properties, and disable or restrict event comments until patching is confirmed.

  • A malicious comment can execute before moderation because WordPress provides the commenter a URL that immediately displays their own pending comment.
  • The patch version must be checked to four decimal places: 6.17.4 remains vulnerable, while 6.17.4.1 is fixed.
  • The article’s observed asset set reflects sites fingerprinted as running The Events Calendar and potentially exposed, rather than confirmed vulnerable or exploitable systems.
  • The article attributes much of the exposure risk to fragmented ownership of secondary public websites, including agency-managed, acquired, staging, and pre-production sites that organizations may not know they own.

A serious flaw in The Events Calendar, a widely used add-on for WordPress websites, could let an outsider take control of the computer running a site without needing an account or password. It affects sites using version 6.17.4 or older when visitors can post comments on event pages, including public event, training, recruitment, and community websites. Organizations should update to version 6.17.4.1 and review lesser-known public websites, because these smaller sites are often managed separately and may be missed during routine updates.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a critical pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerability in a widely deployed WordPress plugin, with public proof-of-concept code and affected versions through 6.17.4. Exploitation requires event-page comments to be enabled and visible, and observed exploitation was low at publication, but affected organizations should prioritize patching to 6.17.4.1.

Socket has hired Jerod Santo, a longtime developer and podcaster, as its new Head of Media. He plans to encourage deeper discussions about growing risks in the shared software components that developers include in their projects. This matters because attacks on those components are becoming more frequent and damaging, while artificial intelligence is helping both criminals find weaknesses and defenders fix them. Developers and organizations everywhere may be affected when the software they rely on contains hidden problems.

Optional · 35 research 14 Sep 2026 16:07 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Human Risk Management Maturity Model

Living Security’s Human Risk Management Maturity Model offers organizations a roadmap to progress from basic security awareness to proactive, data-driven management of cyber risk arising from human employees and AI agents.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The Human Risk Management Maturity Model is a strategic framework for helping organizations move from basic security awareness to a proactive, data-driven discipline.
  • 02The model is designed to identify and reduce cyber risk arising from decisions made by both humans and AI agents in a blended workforce.
  • 03The framework evaluates organizational progress across culture, technology, and process dimensions.
  • 04Its culture dimension focuses on leadership alignment and workforce engagement to manage human and agentic behavior.
  • 05Its process dimension shifts organizations from reactive, one-size-fits-all training toward predictive risk management and outcome-based metrics.

Living Security provides the Human Risk Management Maturity Model as a strategic framework for organizations. The model is intended to help them move beyond basic security awareness toward a proactive, data-driven discipline. It addresses cyber risk created by decisions made by both people and AI agents in a blended workforce.

The framework measures progress across culture, technology, and process. Its culture dimension emphasizes leadership alignment and workforce engagement, while its technology dimension calls for AI-native platforms and deep ecosystem integrations to provide continuous visibility and control. Its process dimension promotes a shift away from reactive, one-size-fits-all training toward predictive risk management and outcome-based metrics.

  • The model treats AI agents as a source of decision-driven cyber risk alongside human workers, rather than limiting human-risk management to employee behavior.
  • It frames mature risk management as requiring continuous visibility and control through AI-native platforms and deep integrations across an organization’s technology ecosystem.
  • The proposed shift from uniform training to predictive management and outcome-based measures makes risk reduction, rather than training completion, the intended measure of progress.

Living Security published a paper that gives organizations a step-by-step model for improving how they handle online safety risks caused by people’s decisions and by AI tools. It focuses on building leadership support and worker involvement, using connected technology to see risks continuously, and replacing identical training for everyone with help tailored to likely risks. This matters because organizations can reduce the chance of harmful online incidents by recognizing and addressing risky behavior before it causes damage.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is an evergreen white paper promoting a maturity framework for managing risk from human and AI-agent decisions, not reporting a specific incident, threat operation, or urgent technical finding. It may be useful for security-program planning but is low priority for time-sensitive security operations.

code execution technique

commit 8457d13a other

Artificial intelligence systems from OpenAI that can perform multi-step tasks using tools or software services.
